business_model.basis: Stated directly in the 20-F Item 4 description of the company.
business_model.claim: Euroseas is a pure containership company that provides worldwide ocean-going transportation services by owning and operating feeder and intermediate containerships that transport dry and refrigerated containerized cargoes.

Our containerships transport dry and refrigerated containerized cargoes, mainly including manufactured products and perishables.

business_model.basis: Stated in the 20-F Item 5 discussion of voyage expenses.
business_model.claim: Under time charter contracts the charterer pays voyage expenses (port, canal, fuel), whereas under voyage charters the company bears those costs.

business_model.basis: Stated in the 20-F Item 5 'Factors Affecting Our Results of Operations' and reflected in the income statement line items.
business_model.claim: The principal operating costs are vessel operating expenses (crew, insurance, repairs, spares, tonnage taxes), dry-docking expenses, vessel depreciation, related-party management fees, and general and administrative expenses.
quotes: Vessel operating expenses include crew wages and related costs, the cost of insurance, expenses relating to repairs and maintenance, the costs of spares and consumable stores, tonnage taxes and other miscellaneous expenses.

business_model.basis: Stated in the 20-F Item 5 and quantified in the income statement (F2).
business_model.claim: The company pays technical and commercial management fees to its affiliate Eurobulk and chartering commissions to Eurochart, a company affiliated with its CEO, creating related-party cost obligations.
quotes: We pay commissions on all chartering arrangements of 1.25% to Eurochart, a company affiliated with our CEO, plus additional commission of usually up to 1.25% to other brokers involved in the transaction, plus address commission of usually up to 3.75% deducted from charter hire.
These are the fees that we pay to our affiliated ship manager (Eurobulk) under our management agreements for the technical and commercial management that Eurobulk performs on our behalf.

business_model.basis: Stated in the 20-F Risk Factors (Item 3.D) discussion of cyclical nature, supply/demand, and over-supply.

competitive_position.claim: The feeder and intermediate containership segments in which Euroseas operates have a significantly smaller orderbook as a percentage of the existing fleet and an older age profile, which management expects will result in very modest fleet growth or even fleet shrinkage in those segments.

competitive_position.basis: Stated in 20-F Risk Factors (P2), citing industry sources, as of April 15, 2026
competitive_position.claim: The worldwide containership fleet grew by 7.1% in 2025 and 5.9% in 2026, with approximately 36.58% of fleet capacity on order, creating over-supply risk that could reduce charter rates.
quotes: the containership fleet increased by 4.5% in 2021, 4.0% in 2022, 8.3% in 2023, 10.1% in 2024 and 7.1% in 2025. As of April 15, 2026, containership volumes have increased by 5.9% in 2026.

the capacity of the fully cellular worldwide container vessel fleet, as of April 15, 2026, was approximately 33.29 million teu with approximately another 12.18 million teu, or about 36.58% of the fleet capacity on order.

competitive_position.basis: Stated in 20-F Risk Factors (P2) and CEO commentary (P8)
competitive_position.claim: Geopolitical disruptions including Houthi attacks in the Red Sea, the effective shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz, and the conflict between the United States, Israel and Iran are cited as factors supporting current container rates but creating uncertainty about their duration.
quotes: Container shipping markets experienced substantial gains in 2024 and 2025, driven by rerouting away from the Red Sea, Gulf of Aden and Suez Canal due to Houthi attacks on ships. These disruptions have resulted in inefficiencies and support for container rates, which may not continue once these are resolved.

the current war in Iran is likely to avert the passage of ships through the Strait of Hormuz; therefore, the container shipping market is likely to face equal challenges in 2026, as it remains unclear when such disruptions will be resolved.

competitive_position.basis: Stated in CEO commentary in 6-K press release (P8), dated August 14, 2026
competitive_position.claim: Management explicitly identifies that the eventual reversal of Red Sea and Hormuz inefficiencies, together with absorption of the increased fleet orderbook, presents challenges for the containership sector over the medium term.
quotes: The eventual reversal of these inefficiencies, together with the absorption of the increased fleet orderbook, presents challenges for our sector over the medium term.

competitive_position.claim: U.S. tariff actions and trade restrictions, including the 34% tariff on Chinese imports announced in April 2025 and subsequent global tariffs of up to 15%, create uncertainty that could reduce containership trade demand.
quotes: In April 2025, tariffs were announced on many U.S. trading partners, including 34% tax on imports from China, 20% on products from the E.U., and a baseline 10% tax on imports from many countries. These tariffs were struck down in February 2026 by a Supreme Court ruling and new global tariffs of up to 15% for up to 150 days were imposed.

competitive_position.claim: China's economic growth stagnated in 2025 and is projected at 4.4% in 2026 and 4.0% in 2027, posing a demand risk given that a significant number of Euroseas port calls involve loading or discharging in the Asia Pacific region.
quotes: Growth was stagnant in 2025 as higher U.S. and EU tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, batteries and other strategic exports weighed on external demand, while ongoing weakness in household consumption, subdued business investment and continued stress in the real estate sector further dampened overall economic momentum. Projections now show a Chinese growth of 4.4 percentage points in 2026 and further growth of 4.0 percentage points in 2027.

competitive_position.basis: Stated in 20-F Risk Factors (P2); the 20-F vessel table (P1) notes fair values exceeded carrying values as of Dec 31, 2025
competitive_position.claim: The company's secured loan agreements contain financial covenants tied to vessel market values, including maximum fleet leverage and minimum loan-to-value ratios, meaning a decline in vessel values could trigger covenant breaches and restrict cash or lead to foreclosure.
quotes: there is a maximum fleet leverage covenant that is based, in part, upon the market value of the vessels securing the loans, as well as requirements to maintain a minimum ratio of the market value of our vessels mortgaged thereunder to our aggregate outstanding balance under each respective loan agreement.

competitive_position.claim: Liner companies, the largest contingent of containership charterers, face significant financial pressure, increasing Euroseas's counterparty risk.
quotes: Liner companies, which comprise the largest contingent of charterers of containerships, have been placed under significant financial pressure, thereby increasing our charter counterparty risk which may have a material adverse effect on our business, financial condition and results of operations.

approximately another 12.18 million teu, or about 36.58% of the fleet capacity on order

The segments in which we operate—feeder and intermediate containerships—not only have a significantly smaller orderbook as a percentage of the existing fleet but also have an older age profile. This is likely to result in very modest fleet growth, or potentially even fleet shrinkage, in these segments.

risks.claim: Euroseas is a Marshall Islands corporation exempt from many Nasdaq corporate governance requirements, and pays commissions of 1.25% to Eurochart (affiliated with the CEO) plus related party management fees of $7,995,498 to Eurobulk in 2025, creating structural conflicts of interest.
quotes: we are exempt from many of Nasdaq's corporate governance practices other than the requirements regarding the disclosure of a going concern audit opinion, submission of a listing agreement, notification of material non-compliance with Nasdaq corporate governance practices, and the establishment and composition of an audit committee and a formal written audit committee charter.

We pay commissions on all chartering arrangements of 1.25% to Eurochart, a company affiliated with our CEO, plus additional commission of usually up to 1.25% to other brokers involved in the transaction, plus address commission of usually up to 3.75% deducted from charter hire.
